idiom_name: hand-written behaviour class with JavaFX ObservableValue properties and explicit listener registration
implementation_notes: Java has no host-invoked unit, so the pattern is built by hand: a reusable behaviour or state-holder class holds its state in JavaFX property objects (DoubleProperty, ObjectProperty and so on), exposes them through the documented get/set/property-getter convention, and consumers attach ChangeListener or InvalidationListener callbacks - the Oracle tutorial notes that a ChangeListener forces eager recomputation while invalidation events can stay lazy, which matters when bindings are wired. Delegation replaces the classic wrapper structure: components receive the behaviour object instead of extending a base control or being wrapped by an adapter, and Bindings/fluent expressions mirror derived values. The cost is explicit lifetime management: every registration needs a matching removal, bindings must be disposed, there is no scheduler honouring call order, and in non-UI Java the same class is simply a state holder composed by constructor injection. Subclassing remains justified only when the behaviour extends the widget itself (a custom control), not when it merely adds stateful logic.
pitfalls: Registering a ChangeListener forces eager evaluation of lazily evaluated bindings, while an InvalidationListener only signals staleness - choosing the wrong one changes both cost and semantics.
Listeners and bindings are strong references: without explicit removal or binding disposal the behaviour outlives the widget it belongs to.
Observable state must be mutated on the JavaFX application thread; background updates need Platform.runLater or a task so observers never see torn state.
